Possible April 20 (420) Connection to Pot Smoking Sub-Culture In Littleton Tragedy, FRC Says

WASHINGTON, April 22 /PRNewswire/ -- Littleton shooting suspects Eric Harris and Dylan Klebold’s connection with April 20 may go beyond its being Adolph Hitler’s birthday. April 20 or "420" is a euphemism or code for smoking marijuana that is "more widespread than ever and still growing ... ‘420’ events are almost worldwide," according to pro-marijuana magazine High Times, reported in April 1999. High Times publisher Mike Edison said, "Every day at 4:20 smokers are indulging. Every year April 20 becomes more and more of an ‘International Burn Day.’" (High Times, April 1999). Also, marijuana is reported to contain 420 different chemicals.

While investigators await toxicology reports

(Marijuananews note: Using the off-hand comment of a traumatized high school student as the basis for this connection, is the worst possible exploitation of a tragedy. The killers were apparently well-known for their admiration of Hitler.

However, the fact that a high school student knew that April 20 has a connection with marijuana tells us that the movement is having an impact. It is unfortunate that it was also Hitler’s birthday.)

"Whether or not these suspects or this incident had any connection to drug use, it is crucial that we recognize what drug use does to our youth

In a 1997-1998 nationwide survey of more than 86,000 high schoolers, the correlation of marijuana use to violence and hopelessness is undeniable:

  • Nearly 76 percent of at least once-a-year pot smokers report carrying a gun to school.
    • (Marijuananews note: This is not even close to the truth. In fact, it is absurd.

    40 percent of DEAland high school seniors smoked marijuana at least once last year. This would mean that 30 percent had carried a gun to school! Actually, only around 3% had done so. Inasmuch as so many students have used marijuana in the last year, it would be amazing if the troubled students who carried guns had never tried marijuana.

    In reality, according to the source cited by the FRC, (see next section) approximately 75% of kids who brought guns to school had used an illegal drug during the last year.

    This is very different from saying that 75% of annual marijuana users carried guns.

    Moreover, the numbers cited immediately below also seem to be deliberately misleading. They apply to kids who brought guns to school, who also had used marijuana or another drug in the last year, not to marijuana users, per se. It is hardly surprising that kids who carry guns would have violent tendencies, without regard to their having used marijuana or another illicit drug in the last year.)
  • Of those users
    • , nearly 70 percent take part in gang activities.
  • Nearly 60 percent think of suicide often or a lot.
  • Nearly 48 percent threaten to harm another.
  • Nearly 63 percent get into trouble with the police.

(Source: PRIDE—Parents Resource Institute for Drug Education)

(Marijuananews note: I emailed the FRC Press Release to PRIDE, the Atlanta prohibitionist propaganda organization. It will be interesting to see if they object to being used in such a big lie technique. See below.)

Ironically, when Bauer announced his candidacy yesterday, he also tried to exploit the Colorado tragedy, but said that he opposes "gun control."

I, too, support the 2nd Amendment, but there is a 100% correlation between these school shootings and guns. Also, 100% of the shooters have been white males. What do correlations prove? Nothing.)

What P.R.I.D.E. really said:

From http://www.prideusa.org

ALMOST A MILLION STUDENTS CARRY GUNS AND OTHER PROBLEMS TO CLASS; SCHOOL ACTIVITIES AND AFTER-SCHOOL PROGRAMS SEEN AS PREVENTIVE

WASHINGTON, June 18 -- Nearly a million students, as young as 10-years-old, carried a gun to school during the just completed school year, and almost half of them (45%) went to school armed on six or more occasions, according to the 1997-98 PRIDE Survey.

Despite these alarming numbers, the percentage of students who say they carried guns to school has fallen by 36% over the last five years from 6.0% in 1993-94, to 4.9% in 1994-95, to 4.5% in 1995-96, to 4.1% in 1996-97, and to 3.8% in 1997-98.
(Marijuananews note: During this time marijuana use has gone up, suggesting a negative correlation between marijuana use and guns in schools. More marijuana equals less guns.)

In addition, the PRIDE study found that involvement in school activities and after-school programs can help to prevent violent behaviors.

Students who did not carry guns to school were 53% more likely to be involved in community-based after-school programs and 34% more likely to be involved in school activities like band and sports teams.

Among the gun-toting youngsters, almost a third (30%) used cocaine once a month or more often, 32% used stimulants such as crystal methamphetamine on a monthly basis, and 31% used hallucinogens monthly. Nearly two-thirds (64%) said they were monthly users of these or some other illicit drug, including marijuana, heroin, inhalants, downers, or designer drugs.

These drug use rates compare to 1.3% monthly cocaine use by students who did not carry guns to school, 3% use of stimulants, and 1.8% use of hallucinogens.
(Marijuananews note: It is interesting that PRIDE did not tell give us the comparison for just marijuana use.)

Over half of the students who carried guns to school (51%) said they had threatened to harm a teacher and almost two-thirds (63%) said they had threatened to harm another student.

"These chilling numbers suggest that for every classroom of 30 students, in every school building in America, on average one student has attended school with a gun in grades six through 12. In nearly half of the classrooms, a student with a gun has been present on six or more occasions. Two out of three of these armed students exhibit hostile intentions and are regular drug users," said Dr. Thomas J. Gleaton, one of the authors of the study.

In a nationwide survey of 154,350 students in grades 6-12, PRIDE found 5,676 students, or 3.8%, who said they carried a gun to school during the 1997-98 school year. Of these, 37% said they carried a gun to school once, 18% carried a gun to school two to five times, and 45% carried a gun to school six or more times.

With more than 25.6 million students in grades 6-12 nationally, 3.8% represents approximately 973,000 students – almost twice the population of Washington, D.C.

Gleaton noted that one percent of the age group that was studied represents more than a quarter of a million students.

"With this volatile mixture of guns, bad attitudes, and drugs, it only takes one student to create a national nightmare like Jonesboro, Arkansas, or Springfield, Oregon," Gleaton said.

Of the students who carried a gun to school, 59% were White, 18% were Black, 12% were Hispanic/Latino, 3% were Asian, and 3% were Native American. Among all students studied (those who carried a gun and those who did not), 79% were White, 10% Black, 6% Hispanic/Latino, 3% Asian, 1% Native American, and 2% Other.

Students who carried guns were less likely to live with both parents (45% vs. 62%) than students who did not carry guns. They were more likely to consider suicide (26% vs. 6%), more likely to be in trouble with the police (74% vs. 22%), less likely to make good grades (37% vs. 68%), and more likely to join gangs (62% vs. 9%).

They were also more likely to use an illicit drug on a monthly basis (64% vs. 15%) and an annual basis (75% vs. 27%).

When they use alcohol and other drugs, students who carried guns to school are far more likely to become very intoxicated or high. Among those who carried guns and drink liquor, 49% said they usually get "very high/bombed/stoned." This compared to 17% of students who do not carry guns.

Of the gun-carriers, 59% said they get "very high/bombed/stoned" when they smoke marijuana, compared to 17% of those who did not carry a gun.
